description: Harmonic Spectra converts many types of data samples into sound. It can be processed for accessability or art!
summary:
Harmonic Spectra in the Earth Information Jukebox transforms scientific Earth data into sound, making complex environmental information accessible through an interactive audio-visual experience.

Our project develops a JavaScript-based sonification system that processes numerical Earth observations and translates them into customizable audio. By applying mathematical transformations and mapping data characteristics such as intensity, temperature, and change over time to musical parameters like pitch, amplitude, and rhythm, users can listen to patterns within Earth's systems. The audio experience is designed to complement visual representations of the same data.
details:
The Earth Information Jukebox turns real-world environmental data into sound and visualizations. Users can select an environmental phenomenon, enter geographical coordinates and a date range, and retrieve measurements. The project processes and normalizes those measurements, maps them to musical frequencies, and generates an audio sequence. It also aims to display the measurements through a graph, timeline, and data table, allowing users to compare what they hear with what is actually happening on Earth.

We used JavaScript: Frontend logic, Python; Backend APIs; Node.js: Server infrastructure; and service orchestration.

HTML and CSS: Website structure and interface design.

NASA Earthdata: Environmental observations, including nighttime lights and lightning datasets.

Web Audio API: Generating musical tones from scientific measurements. GitHub and GitHub Codespaces: Version control, collaboration, and development.

The central idea is essentially scientific sonification: instead of only looking at environmental data, users can listen to it. Each dataset becomes a different kind of musical experience, connecting scientific measurements with sound design.

We considered scientific accuracy, data availability, geographical coordinates, date ranges, normalization, and how to translate numerical measurements into frequencies without losing their underlying meaning. We also considered accessibility, user experience, performance, and the differences between environmental datasets.

We're planning to add Desmos features to the graph as well as accessability, expanding to more datasets in the future.
